en: *Supplementary Meanings of the Commentary on the Lanpen (Bao Ran) Ritual* (with Preface).
Recorded by the Disciple Rixin, who was granted the purple robe, of Pujing Temple in Xi溪, following his listening to the lectures.
These supplementary meanings generally clarify the citations from the *Shuchao* (Commentary), the differences in phonology and meaning, and guide others.

I, the later descendant, recognize the intended purpose [of these works]. I have examined how former masters compiled and refined [the terminology], providing occasional explanations for difficult points (as recorded in the *Pu-ning Lǜ-shī Huì-cuì Jì* and the *Míng-yì Dà-shī Suí-nàn Jiě*), as well as how they extensively collected supplementary definitions and illustrations (as described by the Great Master Jing-jue in the *Míng-yì* and by the Kāñcī Ācārya in the *Shí-yí Tú*).
Their intersecting expositions are too numerous to enumerate in full; however, where there were meanings worthy of adoption, I have likewise adopted them, yet only... [the text here is incomplete].
I have merely rectified the phrasing and meaning; although the chapters and sentences are incomplete, they remain a remnant of former records.
Therefore, I have collectively titled this work *Lanpen Shuchao Yuyi* (Supplementary Meanings to the Commentary on the Lanpen Rite).

It was commenced on the full moon of the sixth month in the first year of the Xining era, the year of Wushen, and concluded on the twelfth day of the seventh month. Consequently, it was re-carved, and I have composed this preface for it.
This commentary, along with its preface, describes the strengths and weaknesses of the *Jiaochao* (Excerpts) and the origins of the *Zhuhua* (Gathering the Flowers).

If this is the case, the single preface is also divided into two sections: the first section, concerning the strengths and weaknesses of the *Jiaochao*, extends from the opening text to the phrase "difficult to master";
the second section, concerning the origins of the *Jiaochao*, extends from the words "this commentary" (*si shu*) down to the end of the preface.
Qiantang was formerly the ancient Yuhang Commandery; it was renamed Hangzhou during the Tang dynasty.
The *Record of Qiantang* states that in the past, Hua Dexin, the Commandery’s Director of Works, established this embankment to prevent the seawater from flooding the land.

He initially issued a recruitment notice stating that anyone capable of bringing one *hu* of earth or stone would be rewarded with one thousand coins. Within ten days, people gathered like clouds; yet before the embankment was completed, he vanished in a supernatural manner.
He no longer took any soil, but discarded it all and departed; thus the embankment was successfully completed.
Zhijuan’s courtesy name was Wuwai, and his sobriquet was Zhongyungzi. His secular surname was Xu, and he was a native of Qiantang.
He received his monastic training at Jingzhu Monastery in his home prefecture and studied the Tiantai teachings under Master Yuanqing of Fengxian, composing ten commentaries on the sutras.
Having mastered ten scriptures, he composed the *Xianju bian* (Collection on Leisurely Dwelling) in sixty fascicles;
his lectures on the Way and his instructions for people are fully detailed in the biographical stele composed by Wu Zunlu of the Jixian Academy, which states:
"Jinshui is the name of a river in Quanjun; because the waters of the Quanjiang join with those of the Wenjiang, it resembles the form of the seal-script character 'jin'."

The characters for "Jin" (晉) were used in their original forms; thus, the name of the prefecture was Jin County and the name of the river was Jin River, exactly as stated in the *Biography of the King of Min*.
Jingyuan, whose courtesy name was Bochang and sobriquet was Qiansou, belonged to the Yang clan and was a native of Quannan; he opened the gate of the Dixin Monastery.

The *Sanche lizhuan* (Biographies of the Three Chariots), the *Xianshou zhuan* (Biography of Xianshou), and the *Huafan qizu zhi yixue wenrou jianjing zhulun* (The Grove of Writings on the Doctrinal Studies of the Seven Patriarchs of China and India, with Annotations on Sutras and Commentaries) are all fully contained within the *Chujia lingxue zhuan* (Biography of the Transmission of Learning for Monastics);
only this brief biography was separately compiled by Rixin.
The "Re-engraving of the Revised Sections" has two intentions: first, to excise the sectional headings and re-engrave the printing blocks;
second, to correct the text of the *Commentary* (*Chao*), including the passage on taking refuge in the Triple Gem and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the record of the *Commentary*":

"record" (*ji*) refers to the *Commentary* itself, such as the *Yanyi Chao*, which is a commentary on the *Huayan Shu*; "pen-shuo-ji" (a record of editorial emendations) is an explanation of the *Qixin Lun*.
The *Xinshu* (Commentary on Faith) is like Kong Yingda’s *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning), which exists to explain the annotations of the Five Classics;
it is not merely a record of extensive excerpts or abridgments.
It is both profane and obstructive—having already become confused and disorderly, it is further characterized by stagnation. It is the work of my contemporaries.

"Having nowhere to place one's hands and feet" means to have nowhere to set them down. The *Analects* states: "If punishments do not accord with the middle way, then there is nowhere to place one's hands and feet.

Now, it is said that this commentary suffers from the faults of being either redundant or too concise; thus, although students may open it and study it repeatedly with their own hands, they will not put it into practice for long.
Therefore, it is said that there is nowhere to place one's hands and feet.
"It is difficult to achieve. In the *Analects*, Ziyou said, "My friend Zhang is one who achieves what is difficult to achieve.
Bao’s commentary states: "This means that the deportment and appearance of Zizhang are difficult to emulate."
The Dharma Master Chuan’ao was surnamed Han and was a native of Qixian County in Bingzhou. Originally a Confucian scholar, he had previously passed the local examination;
later, upon meeting the śrāmaṇera Qianhui—a senior disciple of Chan Master Dinghui—he shaved his head and received the Way.
His mastery of both Buddhist and secular classics was such that he possessed detailed commentaries on all of them, as fully recorded in his original biography.
The Dharma Master was extensively versed in the teachings and served as a teacher who regulated the conduct of others; he produced the *Pāpa-śodhana-śāstra*.
"Ordinary" (*yōngcháng*) means commonplace. "Trained and circumspect" (*xúnxún*) means compliant.
He did not clear away the overgrown weeds; that is, he did not attempt to measure or categorize the vast, desolate wilderness of delusion.
"Whenever I engaged in the task of 'penning and excising' (bi-xiue), I acted with autonomy. That which was correct I recorded with the pen; that which was incorrect I excised and removed.
'Transmitting and shifting' (bo-qian) their texts—'transmitting and shifting' here means deleting; if the text was prolix, I would delete it, corresponding to the word 'excise' used above."
"Seam it up" (*míféng*) means to mend and patch; where there are omissions or deficiencies, one supplements them—this corresponds to the word "pen" (*bǐ*) mentioned above.
"Transmit it to the young and ignorant" (*zhu zhū tóngméng*): "zhū" refers to children who are still immature and deluded. As the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyī*) says: "The young and ignorant seek me."
This is indeed profound.
Regarding "gathering the essence" (*yinghua*): Liu Xie says it means "collecting the essence," while Ban Gu says it means "the essence manifests outwardly.
This is likely close to the intended meaning. The principle of the *Zhongyong* (Doctrine of the Mean) is that speech should be neither prolix nor overly concise.
"Lacking acuity in talent and insight" means that one's talent, literary flair, understanding, and wisdom lack quickness. Although it says "talent and insight," learning is included therein.
To be "deficient in self-insight" means that one's own shallow abilities still arise from one's own perspective; this expresses a hope [for improvement].
The phrase "the illness of later generations" refers to the faults of contemporary people who pluck at the flowers [of superficiality] while debating right and wrong.
This is just as those of today look back upon the past; it is also like the saying from the *Shiji*:

"The illness of the present is Qin, just as Qin looked upon the past. The first two lines of this passage derive their rhetorical force from that text, which states: "The illness of the present is Qin, just as Qin looked upon the past."

When King Wu of Zhou defeated Zhou, he enfeoffed the descendants of Shang; Micizi was granted this land to establish the state of Song. Our Great Ancestor received the Zhou’s enfeoffment from this place and subsequently ascended like a soaring dragon. Therefore, the territory where he received his enfeoffment and rose to kingship was adopted as the dynastic name for his rule over all under heaven. It is also... It is like Emperor Gaozu of the Tang, who received the mandate from the Sui to establish the state of Tang and ascend the throne as Emperor; thus, the realm was named the Great Tang.
For three generations—Taizu, Taizong, and Zhenzong—their virtues were like jade leaves joined in fragrance.
The Imperial Majesty’s True Doctrine and Sacred Procession:
Emperor Wu of Han performed sacrifices to Houtu at Fenyin; the site was established south of the water, which is called "yin" (the dark side).
The following year was the *xinhai* year.
The term *saṃvatsara* refers to the planet Jupiter (*bṛhaspati*), which completes one revolution annually.

Regarding the six types of *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive compounds), the Tripiṭaka Master of Tang China stated: "The *karmadhāraya* (descriptive compound), *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound), *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound), *avyayībhāva* (indeclinable compound), *dvigu* (numeral compound), and *dvandva* (copulative compound)—these six are called *vyadhikaraṇa-tatpuruṣa* (non-co-referential compounds).
One should understand that while the *samāsa* (compound) takes the form of a combination (*saṃyoga*), the analytical member (*vigraha*) does not constitute the actual characteristic of this dharma."
When studying, be careful not to speak from mere conjecture.

The term "dependent designation" (*yīzhǔ chēng*) refers to the fact that the Sūtras are superior while the commentaries (*shù*) are inferior, just as a minister depends upon his sovereign; thus it is called a "dependent designation" (the final character is pronounced in the departing tone).
This is stated in the ten-fascicle *Wénxīn diāolóng* compiled by Liu Xié, which discusses the mental application required for literary composition. The *Dàxué* (Great Learning) refers to this as...
The "Carving of Dragons" (Diao-long) in elementary learning is called "Carving of Insects" (Diao-chong).
"Shu" means to spread out; when a minister submits a memorial to the Son of Heaven, it is called a "shu.
A "ti" (heading) is that which summarizes the proximate meaning within the title; by "capping" the title, one extracts the remote purport from the body of the text to explain the proximate meaning.
Yang Xiong, in his *Yantong*, said: "The words of the Sage are as distant as heaven; the words of the worthy are as near as earth.
Emperor Ling of the Han was the eleventh ruler of the Later Han; his taboo name was Hong.
The *Han shu* was compiled by Ban Gu; it was annotated by Ying Shao and others in the *Jijie*, and Yan Shiguo further provided sub-commentaries.
Thus, "Luzi" was his ancestral title; it was a rank of the Zi (Noble) grade.
The cases are analogous: taking Nan-chong Commandery as an example for Lu-chiang Commandery, and using the state of Ch'ung as an example for the state of Lu.
The states of antiquity are the prefectures (chou) of today; the vassal states of antiquity are the counties (hsien) of today.
"Name" (*ming*) refers to what is called; "taboo" (*hui*) refers to avoidance. One has a name while alive, but one avoids it after death.
*Jianzhong* was the era name of Emperor Dezong; *Huichang* was the era name of Emperor Wuzong.

Regarding "monastic age" (*sengla*) and "Confucian ritual": taking the end of a year as a "lunar month" (*la*), in the Buddhist teaching, only the end of a single summer retreat constitutes a [lunar] month.
"Là" (Lunar Sacrifice).

To posthumously confer a title after an interval of time is called "posthumous enshrinement" (*zhuìshì*); it is a change of name. "Enshrinement" (*shì*) signifies [character]; it also represents the good and evil deeds performed throughout one's life.
The location where he resided during his ordinary life—Mount Guifeng in Zhongnan—is clarified in the *Ruzhixiuji*.
As for the author, [the name] "Sheng" and so forth appears in the *Lueji*; this is merely a citation from Liu Xie’s *Zhishu* (Culling the Flowers).

If the "Noble One" mentioned below appears in the *Analects*, [the Master] privately compared himself to Laozi and Peng Bo, saying: "Laozi and Peng Bo were virtuous high officials of the Yin dynasty who delighted in recounting ancient matters;
I am like Laozi and Peng Bo, merely recounting them."
Regarding the recording of commentaries and sub-commentaries on the sutras: formerly, I received the original commentary by Qingliang (Chengguan) and annotated it for the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

Now, I have again recorded the commentary by Guifeng (Zongmi) and annotated it here for this sutra. This is because I follow the tradition of this school, wherein all explanatory words are appended beneath the text of the sutra and treatise regarding the methods of contemplation (*guanfa*).
In this way, it not only enables students to reach the essential meaning upon encountering the text, but furthermore...
It also establishes the organizational principles for the scriptural treasury with systematic order.

The *Baïhù tōng* was produced during the reign of Emperor Xiaozhang of the Later Han dynasty when he convened a group of Confucian scholars in the Baïhù Hall to discuss the similarities and differences among the Five Classics.
Ban Gu, whose courtesy name was Zǐjiān, received an imperial decree to compile these proceedings and submitted them in ten volumes.
At the Great Beginning (*Taichu*), the primal qi first sprouted; at the Great Commencement (*Taishi*), form and qi first took shape;
at the Great Purity (*Taisu*), the substance first emerged. Broadly explained, there are five; briefly distinguished, there are three.
As for those who claim that [the former] merely plucks at the flowers [of superficiality], this is the deluded talk of those with shallow understanding—how could it be worth believing?
Once the clear and the turbid had been separated, Xu Zheng said: "Yang and clarity constitute Heaven; Yin and turbidity constitute Earth.

From their essence, light is emitted and spread forth as the sun and moon—the essence of the Great Yang and the Great Yin. 'Light' refers to the luminaries, namely the five planets, the twenty-eight lunar mansions, and so forth."

"Dùwù shīshēng" (度物施生): "Dù" (度) is pronounced with the *dài* (待) and *luò* (洛) finals; "shī" (施) is in the departing tone (*qùshēng*). This means to measure and categorize the myriad things and to bestow upon them growth and development.
"Shìjīn" (適今):
"shì" (適) is synonymous with "jìn" (近), meaning "near."
"The constant way of Heaven" means that Heaven possesses constant luminosity.
"The righteousness of Earth" means that Earth possesses constant benefit.
"Yuan Shen Qi" (The Pivot of Summoning the Spirits) refers to the matters of invoking and harmonizing with the divine and spiritual; this is the commentary by Song Jun.
Regarding sentient beings, it is said that the consciousness-principle (vijñāna) has no beginning; within the ālayavijñāna, filial piety is already fully present.

Regarding the vessel-world (bhājana-loka), its characteristics of formation and destruction rub against one another until it is extinguished. Because the vessel-world forms and then again disintegrates, it is said that their characteristics "rub against" one another.
"Huai" (to embrace) means to contain; "ren" (to bear) refers to the earth's ability to contain and sustain all things; "jiao" (exchange) signifies mutual transformation and transition.
"Jiyi" is the title of a chapter in the *Liji* (Book of Rites), which records the principles of offerings and presentations made during sacrifices.
Zengzi’s surname was Zeng, his given name was Shen, and his courtesy name was Ziyu.
"Without morning or evening" means that there is neither beginning nor end.
The source of this phrase differs: it appears as "originating from Chaos" in the *Yuan shen qi*, and as "blocking heaven and earth" in the *Ji yi*.
Together they form a single meaning: the meaning of profound verticality. "Xiao" (孝) means filial piety;
"di" (弟) is pronounced "ti" (悌), referring to the title of rank for the Son of Heaven. A "Wang" (王) is one who takes Heaven as father and Earth as mother.
A "Gong" (公) refers to the lords of the various states. A "Hou" (侯) is a ruler; it refers to the sovereigns of the feudal states.
The "Cheng" (Noble) chapter concerns the high ministers; the "Mingshanli Da" (Illuminating Good Principles for the Great) chapter concerns the advancement of men.
There were nine *qing* and twenty-seven *dafu* according to the *Wangzhi*, but they are now combined and distinguished here because their filial conduct was identical.
"Shi" refers to the service of an officer; it is a designation for one who bears responsibility for affairs.
"Shu ren" means the common people, referring to the multitude of people throughout the world.

As for those who suffer from being unable to reach [this standard], such cases have never existed. The *Xiaojing Shu* (Commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety) states: "There may be some who suffer from eye ailments and are thus unable..."
Furthermore, there has never been one who was filial and yet failed [to receive such signs].
Regarding the *Tianlong futu*, the *Hetu* states: "When Shun ascended the throne as Grand Marshal, he stood with the Three Dukes to observe the Yellow River.
A yellow dragon of five colors emerged before Shun, bearing a chart."
The *Songshu* (Book of Song) states that a divine tortoise emerged from the earth bearing a book for Yu;
it contained the "Method of the Nine Numbers" (*shǔjiǔfǎ*), which is precisely the "Nine Categories" (*jiǔchóu*) of the *Hòngfàn*.

It says that celestial calamities were extinguished; "calamity" (*niè*) refers here to natural disasters. The *Huáinánzǐ* states that Yao shot down the ten suns, removing nine while leaving one behind.
First, the *Shangshu* states: "Virtue moves Heaven," and thus calamity is transformed into fortune.
Regarding the appearance of auspicious clouds (*jingyun*), the *Jiu Tang Shu* records that on the day Emperor Ruizong ascended the throne, auspicious clouds appeared as a sign of divine favor.
Furthermore, during the reign of Emperor Dezong, Li De, the Prefect of Zhezhou, presented a painting of the celebratory clouds (*qingyun*).
In the marshy forests, luxuriance flourished; upon close inspection, it was seen that the trees grew in mutual harmony, their trunks entwined without separation.
Floating treasures unfolded like the story of Guo Ju, who buried his son to preserve his mother, whereupon Heaven bestowed upon him gold.

Extraordinary plants blossomed like the case of Liu Junshu’s grandmother, who, while grieving for her grandson in winter, longed for *jin* (polygonatum); her lament moved Heaven, and *jin* sprang up to fill the ground—thus it is recorded in the *Erya*.
It is said that *kǔjǐn* is the same as *cài*.
A river produced divine fish; when Wang Xiang’s mother longed for fish, Xiang lay upon the ice until the water opened, moved by which a pair of carp leaped forth.
The profound and the manifest: "manifest" refers to clarity. The *Li* (Ritual) says, "Where there is clarity, there are ritual and music; where there is profundity, there are ghosts and spirits.
The two polarities: "polarities" refers to the images; it distinguishes the forms and images of heaven and earth.
Regarding "filiality arising from the heart," the *Preface to the Classic of Filiality* states: "Filiality arising from the heart has already sprouted.
Regarding "relying on reverence," the *Classic of Filiality* states: "Relying on the service of one's father to serve one's ruler, the reverence is the same."
The *Wenxuan* states that one who is extensively versed in the classics and histories is called a "ru" (scholar).
The Five Constants—benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness—are the way to be practiced eternally throughout ten thousand generations.
"Ben" (originally) and "yu" (with) are words used to terminate a sentence.
Physical form and substance are born from one's parents; as the *Jiyi* (Meaning of Sacrifices) states: "The body is the physical legacy of one's parents.
The "Three Studies" refer here to the Mahāyāna precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

*Jiǜtǒng* (The System of Sacrifices) is also the title of a chapter in the *Lǐjì* (Book of Rites); "tǒng" (system) here signifies "root," as it records the fundamental principles of sacrificial rites and ritual purification.
*Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) was compiled by Liu Xi, a Han dynasty *bóshì* (Erudite).

The *Zhou Shu* (Book of Zhou), in its section on posthumous titles (*shìfǎ*), records that the Duke of Zhou established these instructions for King Cheng. For virtuous conduct, there are virtuous titles;

for instance, one who "assisted in goodness and transmitted sagehood" is called Yao. For evil conduct, there are likewise evil titles; for example, one who "destroyed righteousness and impaired goodness" is called Zhou.
*Erya*: "Er" means near; "ya" means correct. Because it consists of words that are close to what is correct, it is called *Erya*.
"Hao Tian" (Vast Heaven) is the same as "Xia Tian" (Summer Heaven). Guo [Pu] says: when the Yang energy is vast and bright, it is called Hao Tian; in spring, it is called Cang Tian (Azure Heaven);
in autumn, Min Tian (Compassionate Heaven); and in winter, Shang Tian (Supreme Heaven).

The *Zhengshi jian Mao shi zhengyi* states: "During the Eastern Han, Zheng Xuan took those glosses and explanations by the Master Mao that were incomplete or where there were discrepancies, and supplemented them with annotations;
these are called 'jian' (annotations), which serve to recommend and complete the intent of the Master Mao."
Regarding "crime" (*zuì*) and "transgression" (*xìn*): some say that what is manifest is called "crime," while what is hidden is called "transgression.
A calf without horns is called "young" (*tóng*); grain growing late is called "tender" (*zhì*); these terms are used for a person who is small and young.
"Sāngwáng" (喪亡) is pronounced with the "xī" (息) and "làng" (浪) finals.

The first character, "yán" (延), means "to extend to" (*yán* being equivalent to *jí*, "to reach"). When a father dies, one writes in a reply: "I extend [my condolences] to my late father" (*shàng yán xiān kǎo*); when a mother dies, "I extend [my condolences] to my late mother" (*yán xiān mǔ*).
"Qi-chang" (pitying sorrow) means to be moved with a sense of poignant grief. When frost and dew descend and all things wither, one speaks of parents as being like all things that perish;
thus, one feels moved by the season and remembers one's kin.
"Ru-zhan" (moistening) means to be drenched and nourished. A light rain is called "ru."

The appearance of being startled and terrified; just as rain and dew moisten and give birth to the myriad things, the filial son desires that his parents be like those myriad things, springing to life in the season of spring;
therefore it is said, "as if he were about to see them."
